summary: An early 1974 listing of information about ARPANET protocols, with pointers to documents and contacts. It is an old version of a document that was later revised; see RFC 694 for the update.

eli5.summary: This was a directory of who to ask and what to read about the network's rules. It was later replaced by a newer directory.

subtitle: Jon Postel's November 1974 directory of ARPANET protocols, with contacts, documents and status notes.

tldr.problem: By late 1974 the ARPANET had many protocols, mostly experimental, and information about them was scattered across RFCs and online files.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel kept one file that lists each protocol with a contact, its documents, the people involved, a schedule and recent developments, marking official standards with [Official].
tldr.outcome: It is a snapshot of the network's protocol landscape in November 1974, and the metadata lists RFC 694 as updating it.

today: RFC 661 is a snapshot of ARPANET protocol activity in November 1974, and its status is recorded as Unknown. The metadata lists RFC 694 as updating it.

sections.title: What the File Is
sections.content:
RFC 661 by J. Postel of SRI-ARC is a file of information on the protocols of the ARPA Network. The author says an effort will be made to keep it current, but that depends on users telling him about protocol developments or corrections.

It is described as a compendium of all protocol-related activity, most of it with experimental protocols. Those that are official standards have the designation [Official] appended. Where a document is online, a pointer is given, and recent RFCs are online at Office-1 in directory <NETINFO> under names of the form RFCnnn.TXT.
sections.eli5: It is a list of network rules. The ones everybody must follow are marked, and the rest are still being tried out.

sections.title: Layout of the Listing
sections.content:
Protocols are grouped by level: IMP-IMP, IMP-HOST, HOST-HOST, HOST-FRONTEND and PROCESS-PROCESS, followed by PROGRAMS and the National Software Works. Each entry has headings for Contact, Documents, People, Schedule and Recent developments, and many are left blank.

Entries include RFC 660 on changes to the IMP and its host interface, the NCP host-to-host protocol (listed both as [Official] and as an experimental variant), TCP, the Network Voice Protocol, Telnet, FTP, mail, remote job entry and graphics.
sections.eli5: The list is sorted by what the rule is for, and every entry has the same boxes: who to ask, what to read, and what is new.

sections.title: Notable Developments Recorded
sections.content:
For the IMP-Host interface, the link number field was extended from 8 to 12 bits and renamed the message identification field, and message type 6 is now used to indicate a reason for a type 7 (destination dead) message.

For TCP, the specification was completed on August 4th. The entry notes that the addressing field is now used as a 4-bit format, 4-bit network, 16 bit TCP, and 24 bit process and port. For the new Telnet, all hosts were to be running it by 1 January 1974, and the server is to be available on socket 23 decimal (27 octal).
sections.eli5: The list also notes news, such as a field getting bigger, so readers could keep up with changes.

sections.title: The National Software Works
sections.content:
A closing section covers the National Software Works (NSW), which is developing protocols for its use of the ARPA Network. The Procedure Call Protocol is intended to let resources be shared at the subroutine level, and will be used to split NLS into front end and back end components.

The listing names a set of Version 2 documents (PCP, PIP, PSP, PMP, PCPFMT, PCPHST, PCPFRK, HOST, EXEC, FILE, BATCH and LLDBUG) and says Version 2 is substantially different from Version 1 and obsoletes it. A demonstration of the NSW concept is to be performed in July 1975.
sections.eli5: One group was building tools that let programs on different computers call each other's helpers, and the list describes their set of papers.
